name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,290

clue.text: Peak starts to fall under joint initiative

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only the first of each is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A climber worries that a joint project will begin with a fall from a summit.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words after 'starts to' each lend their first letter; Fuji is the famous volcano in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, so it is an example of a mountain summit.

clue.text: Incited blonde grumbling about borders

indicators.note: to border something is to lie alongside and straddle it, so the letters span the join between two words
turning about means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddling the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Someone stirred up a fair-haired person who was complaining about the edges of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The end of 'blonde' and the start of 'grumbling' give DEGRU, which read backwards is URGED.
explanation.definitionFit: To urge someone on is to press or push them to act, the same as inciting them.

clue.text: Impetuosity livens up Messi when playing

indicators.note: playing suggests moving about freely, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: the thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Lionel Messi's rash flair brightens a football match whenever he takes the field.
explanation.walkthrough: Messi, the Argentine footballer, supplies letters rather than a person; the whole of 'livens up Messi' is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns describe acting rashly on sudden urges without stopping to think first.

clue.text: Argument over the untidy home became annoying

indicators.note: something turned over ends up the other way round, so its letters run backwards
an untidy arrangement is jumbled, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: a row is a noisy quarrel
taken as written
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A couple quarrels about the messy state of their house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home' gives IN because being in means being at home; 'wore thin' is an idiom for patience or a joke running out.
explanation.definitionFit: A joke or excuse that has worn thin has lost its appeal through repetition and now irritates.

clue.text: Earl in Wisconsin turned Doctor Strange

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it
something turned round faces the opposite way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: E is an abbreviation for earl
WI is the postal code for the US state
the usual abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A nobleman living in the American Midwest became the Marvel sorcerer Doctor Strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Strange' reads as the Marvel hero, but 'Doctor' belongs to the wordplay and 'Strange' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Weird and strange are close synonyms for something odd or unusual.

clue.text: Farmer managed pop diva

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
Cher is the American singer famed as a diva

explanation.surface: A farmer who once acted as agent for a pop star.
explanation.walkthrough: RAN for 'managed' is followed by the singer CHER.
explanation.definitionFit: A rancher runs a large livestock farm, especially in North America.

clue.text: What Professor McGonagall does with small geeks

blocks.note: in the Harry Potter books she teaches young wizards, including the boy hero himself
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A question about how a Hogwarts teacher deals with little nerds.
explanation.walkthrough: McGonagall teaches Harry at Hogwarts, so she TRAINS POTTER; add S for small. A trainspotter is a British hobbyist who logs train numbers, the byword for an obsessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Trainspotters are the stock example of obsessive enthusiasts, so the word is used for nerds in general.

clue.text: Iris worked with pen to stimulate the imagination

indicators.note: material that is worked is shaped and reshaped, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer called Iris took up her pen to fire readers' imaginations.
explanation.walkthrough: IRIS and PEN together are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspire someone is to fill them with creative ideas, rousing their mind to invent.

clue.text: Awful peaty gin from African country

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the eight letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint about a nasty smoky-tasting gin imported from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' reads as a verdict on the gin but signals the rearrangement of 'peaty gin'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a person or thing originating in Egypt, a nation of north-east Africa.

clue.text: Artificial sole binds to boot

indicators.note: to bind is to hold something wrapped up inside, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A fake sole is fastened onto a boot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boot' seems to be footwear, matching the sole; 'to boot' is an idiom meaning in addition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'to boot' means as well or in addition, the same sense as the adverb.

clue.text: Spoilt son leaves ready to ride

indicators.note: whatever leaves goes away, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: a horse is ready to ride once its saddle is on
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A pampered boy walks out on a horse that has been prepared for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoilt son' looks like one phrase, a pampered child; 'Spoilt' is the definition and 'son' is the letter removed.
explanation.definitionFit: An addled egg is one that has gone rotten, so addled can mean spoilt or gone bad.

clue.text: Cleaner removing clothing to be off colour

indicators.note: clothing is the outer covering, so stripping it takes away the outside letters

blocks.note: a daily is a British term for a cleaner who comes in each day

explanation.surface: A cleaner taking off her overalls because she feels unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: A daily is British for a domestic cleaner; strip its first and last letters and AIL remains.
explanation.definitionFit: To ail is to be unwell or poorly, and 'off colour' is an idiom for feeling slightly ill.

clue.text: Chinese dynasty heard important one’s blown in

indicators.note: what is heard is taken by ear, so the spelling follows the sound

blocks.note: the Han dynasty ruled China for four centuries
key means crucial or important

explanation.surface: A historical note that an important Chinese ruling house was swept in on a wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's blown in' seems to describe an arrival on the wind; it describes a handkerchief, which you blow your nose into.
explanation.definitionFit: A handkerchief is the cloth people blow their noses into, so it is a thing one blows into.

clue.text: One has a meaningful job in publishing

definitions.text: One has a meaningful job in publishing

blocks.clueFragment: One has a meaningful job in publishing
blocks.note: surface reading: someone in the book trade whose work feels worthwhile
setter's reading: a job that is literally all about meanings, compiling them for a dictionary

explanation.walkthrough: 'Meaningful' suggests fulfilling work, but read literally it is work full of word meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A compiler of dictionaries spends every day writing out the senses of words for print.

clue.text: Teach ace duet to dance

indicators.note: dancers move around and change places, so the letters swap positions

blocks.note: the seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to coach a star pair of performers in dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ace duet' is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To teach and to educate both mean giving someone knowledge or instruction.

clue.text: Unknown rubs Coe the wrong way

indicators.note: things done the wrong way are out of proper order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Some nobody irritates Sebastian Coe, the Olympic runner and athletics chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubs the wrong way' is an idiom for annoying, but here 'rubs Coe' is the fodder and 'the wrong way' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An obscure figure is little known or unfamiliar to the public, so the adjective matches unknown.

clue.text: Make a short trip, arguing regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other one, so alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A couple bickering constantly while popping out on a brief errand.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of 'arguing'.
explanation.definitionFit: A run can be a quick journey, as in a run to the shops, so to run is to take a brief outing.

clue.text: Powerful women and men

blocks.note: first meaning: female monarchs
second meaning: the chess pieces, which crossword setters call men

explanation.walkthrough: 'men' seems to be the opposite of 'women', but chess pieces are called men, and the queen is the most powerful piece on the board.
explanation.definitionFit: Queens are female rulers of kingdoms, and also the strongest pieces in chess, which are called men.

clue.text: This author’s introduced to unacceptable idea

indicators.note: something introduced to a thing is brought into it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the setter refers to herself or himself as I; the 's is 'is'
'not on' is an idiom for not acceptable

explanation.surface: A writer confesses to being presented with an objectionable concept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on' is British and colloquial for unacceptable; the setter's I goes in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a thought, belief or concept, a general synonym for an idea.

clue.text: Loud female drunk by noon is producing unpleasant smells

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters are shaken into a new order
by means beside, so one piece is set next to the other

blocks.note: N is short for noon
f, forte, is the musical direction for loud
F is the abbreviation for female
taken as written

explanation.surface: A noisy woman who is already tipsy by midday gives off a bad smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' looks like the link but is part of the rearranged letters. Niff is British slang for a bad smell, and to niff is to stink.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang verb niff means to stink, so it describes giving off a nasty odour.

clue.text: Discharged bishop departs drunk

indicators.note: whatever departs goes away, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: boozed means having drunk a lot of alcohol
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A churchman leaves the diocese in disgrace, sacked for drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discharged' looks like the bishop being fired; it means a liquid seeped out.
explanation.definitionFit: A wound or pipe that discharged fluid let it seep slowly out, which is what oozing is.

clue.text: American Express entertaining staff

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to have them inside your home, so the letters are held within

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A credit card company takes its employees out for corporate hospitality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' reads as employees, but here it is a walking stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A staff is a long stick carried for support, and a cane is a walking stick.

clue.text: United’s front two don’t move or warm up

indicators.note: the front of a word is its beginning, so its opening pair of letters is kept

blocks.note: the first two letters of the word, taken from its front
to freeze is to stop still

explanation.surface: The football team Manchester United's two strikers either stand still or do their warm-up exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front two' sounds like strikers in a football team, but it takes the first two letters of 'United'.
explanation.definitionFit: To unfreeze something is to thaw it, raising its temperature so that it is no longer frozen.

clue.text: Once more check out donkeys in reserve

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: RES is the abbreviation for reserve
asses are donkeys

explanation.surface: A vet looks again at the donkeys kept in a nature reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the three-word phrase at the front; 'reserve' is shortened to its standard abbreviation before the animals go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To reassess is to evaluate or examine again, repeating an assessment.

clue.text: English show contempt for returning team

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
to dis someone is slang for disrespecting them

explanation.surface: English fans jeer at a team coming back onto the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: E plus DIS gives EDIS, which runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport a side is one of the two teams in a match, as in the home side.
